ns1:channel.ns1:title: Communications Earth & Environment
ns1:channel.ns1:description:
Communications Earth & Environment is an open access journal from Nature Portfolio that publishes high-quality research, reviews and commentary in the Earth, environmental and planetary sciences. The papers we publish represent significant advances that bring new insight to a specialized area of research. We also provide a community forum for issues of importance to Earth, environmental and planetary scientists, regardless of sub-discipline.

Our scope covers all areas of the geosciences, climate and environmental sciences as well as planetary sciences, including those at the interface with ecology, sustainability and environmental social sciences. Primary research of interest to the journal includes important insights gained from field work, novel analyses of existing data, numerical or analytical modelling, theoretical studies or laboratory experiments.

We encourage submissions that provide independent confirmation of particularly influential publications.

The submission and review processes are managed by our in-house professional editors supported by our Editorial Board Members, who provide technical expertise across the breadth of the Earth, environmental and planetary sciences. We are committed to rapid dissemination of important research results. Articles are published on a continuous basis to ensure swift communication of findings.

ns1:item.ns1:title: Vegetation groundwater use drives streamflow declines in Colorado River headwaters
ns1:item.content:encoded:
Communications Earth & Environment, Published online: 14 September 2026; doi:10.1038/s43247-026-04045-2

Growing-season temperature regulates summer streamflow in Colorado River headwaters through groundwater-supported evapotranspiration, according to sub-daily observations (showing vegetation shifts to shallow groundwater as soils dry) and four decades of gauge records across 18 catchments.
ns1:item.dc:title: Vegetation groundwater use drives streamflow declines in Colorado River headwaters
ns1:item.dc:creator: Harry Stone
Reed M. Maxwell
ns1:item.dc:source: Communications Earth & Environment, Published online: 2026-09-14; | doi:10.1038/s43247-026-04045-2

ns1:item.ns1:title: Long-term ecological stability in the Pleistocene central Levantine corridor revealed by enamel isotopes from Lebanon
ns1:item.content:encoded:
Communications Earth & Environment, Published online: 14 September 2026; doi:10.1038/s43247-026-03925-x

The central Levant maintained stable Mediterranean seasonality and resource-rich C3 woodlands across multiple glacial-interglacial cycles, acting as a persistent ecological refugium for hominins, based on enamel isotopic records from Lebanon.

ns1:item.ns1:title: Widespread drought-driven declines in streamflows and water quality in the Upper Colorado River Basin during 1998-2022
ns1:item.content:encoded:
Communications Earth & Environment, Published online: 14 September 2026; doi:10.1038/s43247-026-03890-5

Severe droughts reduce streamflow and increase water temperature and specific conductance in the Upper Colorado River Basin, according to a data-driven study analysing meteorological drought impacts on river flow and water quality between 1998 and 2022.

ns1:item.ns1:title: Lebanese faunal legacy collections uncover 400,000 years of woodland resilience and distinct hominin ecological strategies
ns1:item.content:encoded:
Communications Earth & Environment, Published online: 14 September 2026; doi:10.1038/s43247-026-03926-w

Mediterranean woodlands persisted in coastal Lebanon for hundreds of millennia, supporting diverse ungulates and shaping distinct hominin foraging strategies, highlighting ecological contrasts with the southern Levant, as indicated by dating, faunal analysis, dental wear, and landscape modeling

ns1:item.ns1:title: Rapid fluvial response to meter-scale coseismic coastal uplift during the 2024 Noto Peninsula earthquake
ns1:item.content:encoded:
Communications Earth & Environment, Published online: 14 September 2026; doi:10.1038/s43247-026-03919-9

UAV surveys show the Hakka River mouth experienced a lowering of 2 m and knickpoint migration of 770 m upstream over the course of a year as a result of the 3.5 m coseismic uplift from the 2024 Noto Peninsula earthquake.

ns1:item.ns1:title: Amazonian trees under long-term drought exposure are more resilient to El Niño extreme
ns1:item.content:encoded:
Communications Earth & Environment, Published online: 14 September 2026; doi:10.1038/s43247-026-03887-0

Long-term drought exposure enhances Amazon tree resilience to extreme drought through structural adjustments at ecosystem and tree levels, which reduces transpiration declines and enables full recovery, based on El Niño observations and a multi‑decadal throughfall‑exclusion experiment.
ns1:item.dc:title: Amazonian trees under long-term drought exposure are more resilient to El Niño extreme
